Confidence Interval for a Standardized Regression Coefficient

Source: R/ci_src.R
ci_src.Rd

Computes a confidence interval for a population standardized regression coefficient, by the standard t-based approach or the noncentral t approach. A thin convenience wrapper around ci_reg_coef, which is the general engine; for the coefficient in its raw metric use ci_rc.

Usage

ci_src(
  std_reg_coef_j = NULL,
  se_std_reg_coef_j = NULL,
  N = NULL,
  p = NULL,
  R2_Y_X = NULL,
  R2_j_X_without_j = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  R2_Y_X_without_j = NULL,
  t_value = NULL,
  reg_coef_j = NULL,
  se_reg_coef_j = NULL,
  sd_Y = NULL,
  sd_X = NULL,
  alpha_lower = NULL,
  alpha_upper = NULL
)

Arguments

std_reg_coef_j

The standardized regression coefficient, or NULL (the default) when it is given in the units of the data as reg_coef_j or when the other inputs determine it (see Details)

se_std_reg_coef_j

The standard error of the standardized regression coefficient

N

Sample size

p

The number of predictors

R2_Y_X

The squared multiple correlation coefficient predicting Y from the p predictor variables

R2_j_X_without_j

The squared multiple correlation coefficient predicting the jth predictor variable (i.e., the predictor of interest) from the remaining p-1 predictor variables

conf_level

Desired level of confidence for the computed interval (i.e., 1 - the Type I error rate). A level above .999999998, whose tail areas are below 1e-9, is refused

R2_Y_X_without_j

The squared multiple correlation coefficient predicting Y from the p-1 predictor variable with the jth predictor of interest excluded

t_value

The t-value evaluating the null hypothesis that the population regression coefficient for the jth predictor equals zero

reg_coef_j

The unstandardized regression coefficient

se_reg_coef_j

The standard error of the unstandardized regression coefficient

sd_Y

Standard deviation of Y, the dependent variable

sd_X

Standard deviation of X, the predictor variable of interest

alpha_lower

The Type I error rate for the lower confidence interval limit

alpha_upper

The Type I error rate for the upper confidence interval limit. The table records the coverage, 1 - alpha_lower - alpha_upper, as its level and, when the two tail areas differ, the areas themselves, which the line beneath the printed table, results_sentence, and the alpha_lower and alpha_upper columns of tidy() state; with a tail area of 0 the interval is a one-sided confidence bound. A nonzero tail area below 1e-9 is refused (see "Small tail areas" in ci_nc_t).

Value

A 3-row data.frame with columns term, value, prob_less, and prob_greater. The term values are "ci_lower", "src" (the standardized regression coefficient point estimate), and "ci_upper", so the estimate sits between its confidence limits. The prob_less and prob_greater columns report the achieved tail probabilities at each limit when the noncentral t method is used (NA for the estimate row).

Details

For standardized variables, do not specify the standard deviation of the variables and input the standardized regression coefficient for std_reg_coef_j.

The interval needs N, p, and one of these: the coefficient (std_reg_coef_j, or reg_coef_j with sd_Y and sd_X) with its standard error (se_std_reg_coef_j or se_reg_coef_j), with t_value, or with R2_Y_X and R2_j_X_without_j; t_value with se_std_reg_coef_j, or with R2_Y_X and R2_j_X_without_j; or the three squared multiple correlations R2_Y_X, R2_Y_X_without_j, and R2_j_X_without_j. The squared multiple correlations fix the magnitude of the coefficient but not its sign: the positive root is returned, with a warning, as in ci_reg_coef. A call that gives none of these is refused with a condition of class dmar_argument_invalid. The interval is computed by ci_reg_coef, and its conditions name the arguments of this function (std_reg_coef_j, not reg_coef_j). A standardized coefficient larger than 1.1 in absolute value is reported with a warning of class dmar_result_qualified, since a coefficient that large is more often one in the units of the data.

Fixed and random predictors. The standard error of the standardized coefficient, whether given as se_std_reg_coef_j, rescaled from se_reg_coef_j by sd_X / sd_Y, or computed from the squared multiple correlations, treats the sample standard deviations of Y and of \(X_j\) as fixed constants (Kelley & Maxwell, 2003, pp. 315–316). The standard deviation of Y varies from sample to sample in every design, and those of the predictors vary as well when the predictors are random, as they are in most observational studies, so this standard error is approximate either way and the interval does not have exactly its nominal coverage. When the values of the predictors are set by the design, the standard error is, in large samples, too large whenever the population coefficient is not 0, so the interval covers above its nominal level. When the predictors are random, the standard error can be too large or too small, and which it is depends on the correlations among Y and the predictors, not on \(R^2\) alone. In 2,193 two-predictor structures drawn with each of the three correlations uniform between -.9 and .9 (structures whose correlation matrix had an eigenvalue below .02 were set aside), the large-sample standard error of the first coefficient was too small in a quarter of them: in none of the 743 in which the predictors explained at most 30 percent of the variance of Y, in 8 percent of those explaining 30 to 60 percent, 56 percent of those explaining 60 to 80, and 79 percent of those explaining 80 to 90, and in all 70 that explained more than 90 percent. A structure outside that range can reverse the last: with one predictor correlated .96 with Y, a second correlated .1 with Y, and the two uncorrelated (\(R^2 = .93\)), the large-sample standard error of the first coefficient is 2.2 times its sampling standard deviation, and at N = 200 both intervals covered it in every one of 4,000 samples.

In a simulation of multivariate normal data with random predictors (20 conditions with 1 to 4 predictors and N from 50 to 1,000; 4,000 or 20,000 samples per condition, with Monte Carlo standard errors of .001 to .005), the 95 percent interval of this function covered the population standardized coefficient .961 to .998 of the time with a single predictor correlated .3 to .7 with Y; .964 to .979 for coefficients of .34 to .52 among two to four predictors correlated positively with Y and with one another and explaining less than 60 percent of its variance; .952 to .956 in the five conditions whose coefficient was 0 or near it (at most .17 in absolute value); and .955 to .965 for suppressors (a predictor correlated 0 to .1 with Y and .6 to .8 with another). With two uncorrelated predictors that explained 72 and 90 percent of the variance of Y, it covered .982 and .937. The central t interval with the same standard error (that of ci_reg_coef with noncentral = FALSE) covered less: .882 to .952 for the suppressors, and .938 and .881 in the last two conditions. With the values of the predictors held fixed from sample to sample instead (six conditions), this function's interval covered .971 to .998 whenever the coefficient was not 0.

Note

This function calls upon ci_reg_coef in DMAR, but has a different naming scheme. See ci_reg_coef for more details.

To form a confidence interval for the unstandardized regression coefficient, use ci_rc. This function is used to form a confidence interval for the standardized regression coefficient.

Not all of the values need to be specified, only those that contain all of the necessary information in order to compute the confidence interval (options are thus given for the values that need to be specified).

References

Kelley, K. (2007). Confidence intervals for standardized effect sizes: Theory, application, and implementation. Journal of Statistical Software, 20(8), 1–24. doi:10.18637/jss.v020.i08

Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2003). Sample size for multiple regression: Obtaining regression coefficients that are accurate, not simply significant. Psychological Methods, 8(3), 305–321. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.8.3.305

Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2008). Sample size planning with applications to multiple regression: Power and accuracy for omnibus and targeted effects. In P. Alasuutari, L. Bickman, & J. Brannen (Eds.), The Sage handbook of social research methods (pp. 166–192). Sage.

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge. (See Chapter 4 on individual comparisons of means and Chapter 6 on trend analysis.)

Smithson, M. (2003). Confidence intervals. Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage Publications.

Steiger, J. H. (2004). Beyond the F Test: Effect size confidence intervals and tests of close fit in the Analysis of Variance and Contrast Analysis. Psychological Methods, 9(2), 164–182. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.9.2.164

Examples

ci_src(std_reg_coef_j = .6707, .1761, N = 30, p = 6, conf_level = .95)
#>  term     value prob_less prob_greater
#>  ci_lower 0.270 0.025     0.975       
#>  src      0.671 <NA>      <NA>        
#>  ci_upper 1.060 0.975     0.025       
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
